tone.quote: 2.232 Pitch. /0/ datum pitch, a toneme of musical register of the syllable nucleus, on which words spoken in isolation generally begin and end. /1/,/2/,/3/ successively higher pitch tones, of relevance at levels of the grammar above that of the phonological word. /h/ emphatic high pitch toneme, occurs in company of primary clause stress in phonological stress groups marked for emphasis [...] [2.5, fn. 2:] These pitch levels are all relative within an utterance section, varying absolutely from speaker to speaker and even from one part of the utterance to another. Only in chanting is the same musical pitch maintained with any degree of strictness as in any other language (including 'tone' languages).
tone.locator: sec. 2.232 'Pitch', pp. 51-52; sec. 2.5 'Intonation' begins p. 65; footnote 2 is under sec. 2.51.1 on p. 68, not c. p. 66; supporting stress statement sec. 2.1 p. 36
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.says: Pitch is analysed as part of intonation, not of the word: stress falls predictably on the final syllable and is 'not emically relevant' at word level (2.1, p.36); the pitch 'tonemes' /0/-/3/ and emphatic /h/ are 'of relevance at levels of the grammar above that of the phonological word' (2.232) and combine with stress and juncture into Intonation Contours (2.5: declarative, interrogative etc.); pitch levels are relative within the utterance, and the author contrasts this explicitly with 'tone'…
